subject: Capacity corridor proposal for Stellaris committed plan
messages:
From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
To: Emily Zhang <emily.zhang@stellaris.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-10-01T09:14:00Z
Subject: Capacity corridor proposal for Stellaris committed plan

Emily — following our call this morning I sketched a capacity corridor that maps your 3 canonical traffic patterns to committed GPU slabs and burst allowances. Key items up front:

- Baseline committed: 8x A100-80GB equivalents (quantized Llama2-Chat style workloads) for sustained daytime traffic (~2k TPS tokens/sec aggregate after batching).
- Burst pool: shared 4x A100-80GB for 10-minute spikes (covering ~+60% token burst) with automatic fallback to smaller quantized variants if bursts exceed capacity.
- SLO targets: p95 generation latency target is 650ms for the 1k token prompt profile on the recommended model; we recommend a 1.25x headroom factor for peaking and warm-cache assumptions.

I attached a workbook with the token/sec estimates and a short chart of p95 sensitivity across sequence lengths. Please review the assumptions column — the most sensitive knobs are: model variant (FP16 vs 4-bit quant), average prompt length, and cache hit rate for shared prefixes.

Next steps I propose: you confirm weekly peak window (you mentioned heavy batch traffic 11:00–14:00 PT), procurement confirms timeline for committing to the slab, and our infra team (cc'd Karthik) validates mapping to available SKUs in the region.

Thanks — happy to jump back on a 30m technical follow-up.

— Marcus
Director, Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference

Attachment(s): stellaris_capacity_workbook.xlsx
From: Emily Zhang <emily.zhang@stellaris.ai>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ravi Mehta <ravi@stellaris.ai>, Stellaris Procurement <procurement@stellaris.ai>
Date: 2026-10-01T12:03:00Z
Subject: Re: Capacity corridor proposal for Stellaris committed plan

Marcus — thanks for the quick turn. A few clarifications from our side:

1) Weekly peaks: yes, primary spike 11:00–14:00 PT M–F. We also see a smaller evening spike 19:00–20:00 PT.
2) Typical prompt profile: mean prompt 350 tokens, mean response 180 tokens (so ~530 tokens/session).
3) Cold-starts: during ramp-up we expect a 3x transient on p95 for first 30s until KV caches warm.

Procurement asked for a firm SLA fit at commit levels (they want to see how often we might hit burst and what costs look like). Can you add a short table that maps 3 commit tiers (starter, growth, enterprise) to expected p95 under conservative cache assumptions (20% hit rate) and to monthly committed spend?

Also, can your team confirm whether the burst pool auto-fallback would switch to a smaller quantized model in <30s or require a restart? That's key for our latency planning.

Emily
Head of Product
Stellaris AI
From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
To: Emily Zhang <emily.zhang@stellaris.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-10-02T08:46:00Z
Subject: Re: Capacity corridor proposal for Stellaris committed plan

Emily — brief answers inline, and I've updated the workbook (see tab: tiered-sla-estimates).

- Tier mapping (short):
  * Starter: 4 committed A100 equiv, burst +2 GPUs — p95 (conservative cache 20%) ~1.1s for 1k-token profiles; monthly commit est: $58k
  * Growth: 8 committed, burst +4 — p95 ~650–750ms; monthly commit est: $110k
  * Enterprise: 16 committed, burst +8 — p95 ~420–520ms; monthly commit est: $200k

- Fallback behavior: the runtime performs model-family fallback without container restart by routing new requests to the quantized variant already loaded on burst nodes when available. That switch is typically sub-1s for new requests; warmed KV cache differences can add ~50–200ms until prefix caches are reheated. We will not drain existing in-flight KV caches during fallback.

Notes: the p95 numbers assume continuous batching at target concurrency and a modeled 20% cache hit rate for shared prefixes. If your workload has longer shared prefixes (e.g., multi-turn chat threads), effective cache hit could rise to 45% which materially reduces required committed GPUs.

I'll ask Karthik to validate SKU mapping to the us-west-2 pool and also to produce a quick monte-carlo on daily peak variance for the Growth tier.

— Marcus

Attachment(s): stellaris_capacity_workbook.xlsx
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Emily Zhang <emily.zhang@stellaris.ai>, Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-10-03T17:32:00Z
Subject: Re: Capacity corridor proposal for Stellaris committed plan

Emily — quick infra check after mapping the Growth tier to available SKUs in us-west-2:

- Equivalent mapping used: 8 committed A100-80GB equiv = 6x A100-80GB (GPU performance fudge for our quantized kernel mix); burst +4 mapped to a pool of 4x A30s for cost-effective short spikes with quantized models.
- Cold cache behavior: warmup of KV caches tracked in the workbook shows median 12s to 80% prefix hit recovery after a routing change; worst-case observed in our sim was ~45s with many unique prefixes.
- Ops guardrails: we recommend a soft-throttle at 85% committed token/sec to avoid sustained spill to burst; set autoscale cooldown to 60s and a gradual reclaim over 5 minutes to prevent oscillation.

If Stellaris signs Growth (DEAL-4982) with a 60-day onboarding window, we can provision the committed slab and prewarm common model variants before your traffic ramps. Ben will follow up on pricing annex language for the burst policy.

Karthik
Sr. Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
